text: The respiratory system delivers oxygen to the cardiovascular system and removes carbon dioxide. Turbinate bones in the nasal passage filter large air particles, adjust air temperature to body temperature, and house the sense of smell. Smaller airborne particles settle in the trachea and bronchi, triggering coughing to expel them; these areas are protected by epithelium and mucous glands, though some microbes (e.g. Mycoplasma) can break down this defense, letting other microbes attack the lungs. Very small particles like bacteria and viruses can reach the alveoli, where they are normally destroyed by immune cells called macrophages — but some microbes (e.g. PRRS virus) destroy these macrophages, leaving the lungs open to infections such as Pasteurella. Breathing is driven by movement of the intercostal muscles, ribs, and diaphragm; gas exchange happens in the alveoli, with oxygen diffusing into the blood and carbon dioxide diffusing out for exhalation. Key terms: alveolar macrophage (cell in the alveoli that destroys bacteria/viruses), bronchitis (inflammation of the bronchi causing coughing), pneumonia (inflammation/infection of the lungs), pleurisy (inflammation/infection of the pleura, the membranes covering the lungs and chest interior), rhinitis (inflammation of the nasal lining, from gas, dust, or microbes), and tracheitis (inflammation of the trachea causing strong coughing). Normal respiratory rate is 20–40 breaths/min in piglets and 15–20 in fattening pigs and sows, and it increases when the lungs are damaged.
